Diseases caused by Haemophilus influenzae (including beta-lactamase-producing strains), Haemophilus parainfluenzae (including beta-lactamase-producing strains), Streptococcus pneumoniae (penicillin-susceptible strains only), or Moraxella catarrhalis (including beta-lactamase-producing strains): Administer 300 mg orally every 12 hours for 10 days. 2. Acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae (including beta-lactamase-producing strains), Haemophilus parainfluenzae (including beta-lactamase-producing strains), Streptococcus pneumoniae (penicillin-susceptible strains only), or Moraxella catarrhalis (including beta-lactamase-producing strains): Administer 300 mg orally every 12 hours for 10 days. 3. Pharyngitis and tonsillitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes: Administer 300 mg orally every 12 hours for 5–10 days, or 600 mg orally every 24 hours for 10 days. 4. Uncomplicated infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus (including beta-lactamase-producing strains) or Streptococcus pyogenes: Administer 300 mg orally every 12 hours for 10 days. 5. Pediatric dosing for diseases caused by Haemophilus influenzae (including beta-lactamase-producing strains), Streptococcus pneumoniae (penicillin-susceptible strains only), or Moraxella catarrhalis (including beta-lactamase-producing strains): For children aged 6 months to 12 years: Administer 7 mg/kg orally every 12 hours for 5–10 days, or 14 mg/kg orally every 24 hours for 10 days. For children under 6 months: Safety and efficacy have not been established. For children over 12 years or weighing more than 43 kg: Administer 300 mg orally every 12 hours for 5–10 days, or 600 mg orally every 24 hours for 10 days. 6. Pediatric dosing for diseases caused by Streptococcus pyogenes: For children aged 6 months to 12 years: Administer 7 mg/kg orally every 12 hours for 5–10 days, or 14 mg/kg orally every 24 hours for 10 days. For children under 6 months: Safety and efficacy have not been established. For children over 12 years or weighing more than 43 kg: Administer 300 mg orally every 12 hours for 5–10 days, or 600 mg orally every 24 hours for 10 days. 7. Drug interactions with cefdinir: BCG vaccine (live): Cefdinir reduces the efficacy of the BCG vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Administration of live bacterial vaccines should be delayed until antibiotic therapy is completed. Cholera vaccine: Avoid coadministration with systemic antibiotics, as these agents may inactivate the vaccine strain. Do not administer the cholera vaccine to patients who have received antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. Oral microbiota (bacterial spores): Antibiotics may reduce the efficacy of oral microbiota products. Complete antibiotic regimens 2–4 days before initiating microbiota therapy. Aluminum hydroxide and calcium carbonate: These agents reduce cefdinir absorption by increasing gastric pH. Use caution and monitor closely. Amikacin, gentamicin, kanamycin, neomycin, streptomycin, tobramycin, and plazomicin: Cefdinir increases the nephrotoxic and/or ototoxic effects of aminoglycosides. Use caution and monitor renal function closely. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., atezolizumab, avelumab, balstilimab, camrelizumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, toripalimab): Cefdinir may interfere with the therapeutic effects of these agents. Use caution and monitor closely. Azithromycin, clarithromycin, doxycycline, erythromycin (various forms), minocycline, tetracycline: These bacteriostatic agents may antagonize the bactericidal effects of cefdinir. Use caution and monitor closely. Hormonal contraceptives (e.g., ethinyl estradiol, dienogest, levonorgestrel): Cefdinir may reduce contraceptive efficacy by altering intestinal flora. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but additional or alternative birth control methods may be advisable. Probenecid: Probenecid increases cefdinir levels by competing for renal tubular clearance. Use caution and monitor closely. Furosemide and voclosporin: Coadministration may increase the risk of nephrotoxicity. Modify therapy and monitor closely. Warfarin: Cefdinir may enhance the effects of warfarin through an unspecified mechanism. Use caution and monitor coagulation parameters. Ibuprofen: Cefdinir may increase ibuprofen levels through competition for renal tubular clearance. Monitor closely. Rose hips and willow bark: These agents may increase cefdinir levels through competition for renal tubular clearance. Monitor closely. 8. Additional considerations: Cimetidine, famotidine, nizatidine, and sodium bicarbonate: These agents reduce cefdinir absorption by increasing gastric pH. Use caution and monitor closely. Sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid: Antibiotics may reduce the efficacy of this combination by altering colonic bacterial flora required for drug activation. Use caution and monitor closely. Chloramphenicol: This agent may antagonize the effects of cefdinir through pharmacodynamic antagonism. The clinical significance is unknown. Choline magnesium trisalicylate: Cefdinir may increase the levels of this agent through competition for renal tubular clearance. The clinical significance is unknown.
